lessons: Pin the root hard and let freedom grow toward the tip. In the reference, the coils by the trident collar barely move and amplitude rises steadily toward the free end. For Sunbound: give the 1-2 segments nearest the pommel almost no motion, build freedom along the length, and give the tip the most swing.

Keep the weapon still while the cloth moves. The spear never moves while the ribbon animates, so the cloth is the only motion in frame and reads clearly. For the Sunbound idle/inspect showcase, hold the sword steady and let only the streamer move, plus the small guard accent. The secondary motion must not shake the main mesh.

Use a twisting flat strip, not a tube. The ribbon turns between broad face-on sections and thin edge-on sections, which creates rhythm and keeps it from looking like a heavy banner. Model the Sunbound streamer as a thin, slightly thick strip with enough length-wise loops to twist cleanly, and taper or notch the free end to a point like the reference tail.

Vary the free end's poses. Across 3.5-6.2 s the tail moves through clearly different shapes (high upright loop, low swing, wide horizontal, downward flick) rather than one repeated sway. A Sunbound idle loop needs at least 3-4 distinct key silhouettes for the tip, but with much smaller amplitude than the reference (the brief asks for restrained delayed motion that settles).

Make the idle loop seamless. Matching shapes at 3.0 and 6.0 and an apparent 0:03 clip length suggest a loop of about 3 s. Author the Sunbound streamer idle as a closed loop where the first and last frames match. Pick the loop length from your own timing tests, not from this clip.

Don't copy the wrap. The reference ribbon coils the whole shaft, including where a hand would go. Sunbound's brief requires a short streamer attached at the pommel beyond the hand area, with the grip left clear. Take only the root-pinned, tip-loose motion grading, not the full-length wrap or the ribbon's length relative to the weapon.

Scale the free length down. Here the free tail extends roughly 15-25% of the spear's length past the butt and loops above and below the shaft. For Sunbound, keep the free length short enough that, at full swing, the tip never reaches back over the grip or blade. Check this in the upright and side views.

Keep front/back occlusion clean. The coils pass correctly in front of and behind the shaft with no visible clipping in the samples. For the Sunbound streamer near the pommel, check every keyed or simulated frame for interpenetration with the pommel and grip, and add a collider or offset if needed. Whether the reference used collision is unknown.

Supply both a side view and an upright view. The reference pairs an animated side view with a calm vertical composition, where the ribbon hangs in a regular spiral with a short tail below. A matching Sunbound presentation: an animated side view plus an upright settled pose with the streamer hanging calmly below the pommel.

Treat the reference as an artistic target, not a technical spec. Sampled stills at 1 fps and 3 fps can't show the easing, the true speed, the source frame rate or the simulation method. Time the Sunbound streamer by watching your own playback at full frame rate.

Whether the spear has tiny roll or position changes below the tile resolution.
Whether the 7-8 s upright view is a still, a paused video or a slow animation.
Ribbon thickness, whether it is double-sided, and how the texture or shader was built. The pastel mottling is visible, but its channels are not.
Anything in-game: whether the asset runs in Roblox, its performance, how it attaches to an avatar, or how it behaves when equipped or swung. None of this is shown.

videos.rig_and_camera: The footage is a screen recording of the X/Twitter web UI that plays embedded game clips. It is a recording of a recording, with compression, player chrome, and full-screen toggling. Two setups appear. (1) 00:00-00:02: a third-person static showcase camera on a grid baseplate, with white blocky Roblox-style avatars (classic block-body dummies) posed still with weapons attached, plus one free-floating weapon. (2) 00:10-00:19 and about 00:24: a first-person camera with a separate viewmodel. The arms have sleeves and skin-toned hands, not block-avatar arms. The camera is set in a gothic courtyard with a grid floor and a purple blocky target dummy. The viewmodel is one-handed and right of center for the red weapon, two-handed spread for the purple orb plus claw, and two-handed centered low for the cyan pistol. The gameplay HUD (compass, health, hotbar, weapon icon) shows only at 00:17. The camera stays fixed in direction across samples, with no visible look-around. Weapon position changes come from the viewmodel animation, not camera movement. Sampling is too sparse to judge micro sway.
lessons: Reveal structure: one big burst, then a small local glow. In both observed reveals (purple at 13 s, cyan at 15 s), the burst shows up in a single 1 fps sample. One second later only an aura hugging the weapon remains. Make the equip burst a single short event, under a second at most and probably much shorter (exact length cannot be measured from these samples), then settle into a persistent accent far smaller than the burst.

Bursts throw energy away from the weapon: purple rays toward the upper right, cyan tendrils streaking left, dark fragments flung outward. Point Oathsplitter's equip ignition along the inner rails toward the twin points. Have Sunbound's reveal gather inward toward the guard disk and then collapse onto it. Have Warlink's pulse run between the two pommels along the chain.

Warlink connecting pulse: the purple burst at 13 s fills the space between two hands before splitting into two separate local auras at 14 s. Use that for Warlink: a brief bridge between the two cleavers, then local heat at each endpoint or selected links. Keep link gaps readable once settled.

Counterexample for Oathsplitter: the red weapon (10-12 s, 18-19 s) has full-length bloom that hides internal structure and edges in every sample. Do not use that for Oathsplitter. Keep the amber glow in a narrow channel along the inner edges, keep the slot dark and empty in the ready state, and keep bloom radius small enough that the opening reads at viewmodel distance.

Ready-state intensity: the settled cyan glow (16, 17, 24 s) covers only part of the weapon and leaves its silhouette fully readable. That fits the briefs' quiet states: low inner-edge heat for Oathsplitter, a small guard/spine accent for Sunbound, endpoint/link heat for Warlink.

Show vs ready: the third-person showcase auras (0-2 s) are denser and more particle-heavy (sparks, flecks, floating sparkle) than the first-person ready glows. If you build a showcase or inspect mode, it can run hotter, but the first-person ready state should be the restrained version.

HUD safe zones: in the HUD ready frame (17 s), the weapon and glow sit in the lower-center gap between the health bar (bottom left), hotbar (bottom center), weapon icon (bottom right) and compass (top center). Keep settled ready effects out of those zones. Let only the brief reveal burst cross into them.

Viewmodel framing: a one-handed long weapon was shown right of center with its tip in the upper-middle screen and the hand in the lower right. Dual items were spread to the lower left and lower right. For Oathsplitter (two-handed, long), plan for part of the blade to leave the frame and keep the twin points or slot visible during the reveal. For Sunbound, put the guard disk in the lower-center third, where the eye lands. For Warlink, frame one cleaver in each lower corner with the chain sagging between them.

Contrast via dark smoke: the purple and cyan reveals pair a bright core with dark smoke or fragments, which keeps them readable against the pale lavender environment. On amber effects, a little charcoal smoke or ember debris would add value contrast without turning the effect into an opaque white-yellow wall.

Hold one dominant hue per weapon (red, violet, cyan) in both burst and ready states. Across the Incarnam set, keep amber as the single energy hue and vary the spatial structure (inner channel, gathered guard accent, linked endpoints), not the colour.

lessons: Build the hand-separation loop around four readable chain states, as the samples show them: (1) gathered, with the span hidden or bunched; (2) snap-apart, with the chain bowed upward above the line between endpoints (follow-through lag); (3) settle, a shallow mid-span sag; (4) taut, nearly straight at maximum separation. In the reference, bow to straight takes about 0.5-0.7 s, and the full loop is about 1.75-2.0 s (sampling-limited).

Make the taut state the length check. The chain should read nearly straight exactly when the hands reach full separation, so the apparent length equals maximum endpoint distance. Slack should only appear when the endpoints are closer than that length. Never let the chain look straight at two different separations.

The bow at snap-apart curves upward, against gravity. It reads as a delayed reaction to the hands moving, not as gravity sag. Use a lagging upward or outward arc for the first beat of separation and let gravity sag show only in the settle beat.

When the hands gather, the reference hides the span: it drops out of frame in 1P and sits behind the head or between the arm cubes in 3P. At 15.85 the extra length sticks out past one hand instead of sagging deeply. Warlink needs an explicitly designed quiet rest configuration (a short loose drape between the pommels, staying inside the compact length) rather than leaving it to chance.

The reference anchors the chain at the wrists, with one end coiled around the forearm. For Warlink, move both endpoints to the cleaver pommel eyelets and keep each attachment fixed relative to its pommel at every sample. Do not copy the wrist coil, because the brief requires the chain to connect beyond the grip zone.

Close-up links are rigid rectangles with open centres, alternating 90 degrees (flat, then edge-on), at consistent scale along the whole span. In 3P at distance the same chain reads as a dark beaded line. Model full links for 1P and simplify to a bead or line silhouette for distant 3P, keeping the connected curve.

Do not copy the 4.8-7.8 third-person segment's length or behaviour. There the chain is long, whips into large loops and trails past the frame edge, which contradicts the Warlink brief's compact tether and its 'not a long-range whip' rule. Use the 9.2-16.4 two-hand loop as the motion reference.

Under the fire effect, the middle of the span is completely covered and only links right at the hand stay readable. For Warlink's local heat, keep the effect from fully covering the links. Leave link edges or the endpoints visible and let the heat sit on or near the links. The reference fire breaks into embers within about 0.5-0.75 s of sampled time.

In first person at full separation, the chain spans the entire screen width just below the horizon, with the hands at the screen edges. Check that the chain never clips through the camera near plane or covers the crosshair, and that both endpoints stay attached when one hand leaves the view.

Validate the same animation from both a static 1P camera and a behind-and-above 3P camera. The reference shows that the same pose loop gives very different silhouettes: a horizontal span in 1P, an arc over the head in 3P.
Treat all timing from this footage as approximate. It is a re-encoded social-media screen capture sampled at 3-5 fps, so use ranges, not frame-exact keys.
